# The Mechanical Risks of Mixed Tire Diameters on a Single Axle

Driving three tires sized 175/70 R14 and one tire sized 175/65 R14 creates an immediate mechanical imbalance that compromises vehicle dynamics, particularly if the mismatched wheel is located on the same axle as the others. The difference between a 70-series sidewall height and a 65-series sidewall height represents approximately 5% of the total tire diameter (roughly 3.8 cm or 1.5 inches in vertical radius). While this might seem negligible for visual inspection, it introduces significant variables into the suspension geometry and drivetrain load calculations that standard vehicle engineering does not account for during testing.

When four wheels are identical, the contact patch height relative to the hub center is uniform. This symmetry ensures that when one wheel hits a pothole or bump, the other three remain in their expected spatial relationship to the chassis and the opposite axle. Introducing a tire with a different diameter on the same axle breaks this symmetry. If your Hyundai Accent's 175/65 R14 tire is mounted on the front-left, while the remaining three are 175/70 R14, the left side of that specific axle sits lower than the right side by roughly half the difference in height. This effectively tilts the suspension geometry locally, altering the camber angle and potentially inducing excessive stress on ball joints, tie rod ends, and control arm bushings over time.

The consequences escalate depending on whether the vehicle is front-wheel drive (FWD) or rear-wheel drive (RWD). Since many compact cars like the Hyundai Accent are FWD, the drivetrain connects directly to the wheels that bear the steering load. If you mount the smaller diameter tire on a driven wheel, the final drive ratio changes effectively for that side of the car. The differential is designed to split torque equally between two axles rotating at roughly the same circumference. When one axle rotates faster due to a larger diameter tire (the 175/70), the differential must constantly compensate by sending varying amounts of power to each wheel, even on straight pavement where no turning is required. This creates unnecessary parasitic drag and places cyclic stress on the limited-slip differential components or the viscous coupling in RWD vehicles, accelerating wear on gear teeth and bearings.

Additionally, modern stability control systems rely on precise data from ABS sensors regarding wheel rotation speed to detect skids or loss of traction. A significant diameter mismatch generates a false "wheel slip" signal because the smaller tire must rotate faster than the larger tire to cover the same distance per revolution. The Electronic Stability Program (ESP) may interpret this discrepancy as an impending drift or a braking event, leading it to erroneously apply brakes to specific wheels. This intervention can result in unpredictable handling characteristics and reduced effectiveness during emergency maneuvers.

Given that your original 175/70 R14 tire has been driven flat for approximately 16 kilometers, the internal structure is likely compromised beyond repair regardless of size matching. Rubber under extreme heat and stress without pressure undergoes delamination and sidewall separation risks. Attempting to install a temporary mismatched tire alongside three new or correct-sized tires is technically unsafe and violates standard maintenance protocols found in automotive engineering guidelines.

If you require immediate mobility, the safest course of action is not to mix sizes but to remove the damaged wheel entirely and tow the vehicle to a service center for professional repair. Attempting to operate with four different wheels introduces variables that no factory calibration can correct, risking catastrophic suspension failure or loss of control at highway speeds.
